   308	+`references/nv-paper/fullpaper.tex:1096-1100`. -/

   313	+    ∑ u : Fin t → ZMod 2, operatorFourier O u * operatorFourier O u = 1 := by
   314	+  rw [sum_operatorFourier_sq]

   317	+  rw [← Nat.cast_smul_eq_nsmul ℂ]
   318	+  rw [smul_smul]
   319	+  simp

   321	+/-! ## Observable-distance normalization -/
   322	+
   323	+/-- The affine operator `(1 ± S)/2`, which is the effect of a binary projective measurement when `S` is a binary observable.
   324	+The two effects are `(1 + O) / 2` and `(1 - O) / 2`. -/
   325	+noncomputable def binaryObservableEffect {ι : Type} [Fintype ι]
   326	+    [DecidableEq ι] (outcome : Bool) (O : Op ι) : Op ι :=
   327	+  if outcome then ((2 : ℂ)⁻¹) • (1 - O) else ((2 : ℂ)⁻¹) • (1 + O)
   328	+
   329	+/-- The squared binary-measurement distance of two operators, summed over the two
   330	+effects `(1 ± O)/2`; when both operators are binary observables this is the
   331	+squared distance between the associated binary projective measurements.  This is the measurement
   332	+distance calculated in `references/nv-paper/fullpaper.tex:900-912`; its relation
   333	+to `stateDepDistSq` is recorded in
   334	+`docs/paper-gaps/qpbt_linearity-distance-normalization.tex`. -/
   335	+noncomputable def binaryObservableDistSq {ι : Type} [Fintype ι]
   336	+    [DecidableEq ι] (S T ρ : Op ι) : ℝ :=
   337	+  ∑ outcome : Bool,
   338	+    stateDepDistSq (binaryObservableEffect outcome S)
   339	+      (binaryObservableEffect outcome T) ρ
   340	+
   341	+/-- The squared binary-measurement distance is half the squared
   342	+state-dependent operator distance.
   343	+
   344	+**Local fix:** Source equation (3) at
   345	+`references/nv-paper/fullpaper.tex:903-911` ends by identifying the squared
   346	+binary-measurement distance with the squared state-dependent operator distance
   347	+of the two observables; the correct relation carries the factor `1 / 2` proved
   348	+here.
   349	+Documented in
   350	+`docs/paper-gaps/qpbt_linearity-distance-normalization.tex`. -/
   351	+theorem binaryObservableDistSq_eq_stateDepDistSq_div_two
   352	+    {ι : Type} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι] (S T ρ : Op ι) :
   353	+    binaryObservableDistSq S T ρ = stateDepDistSq S T ρ / 2 := by
   354	+  simp only [binaryObservableDistSq, Fintype.univ_bool, stateDepDistSq,
   355	+    binaryObservableEffect, smul_add, Matrix.conjTranspose_sub,
   356	+    Finset.mem_singleton, Bool.true_eq_false, not_false_eq_true,
   357	+    Finset.sum_insert, reduceIte, Matrix.conjTranspose_smul, star_inv₀,
   358	+    star_ofNat, Matrix.conjTranspose_one, Finset.sum_singleton,
   359	+    Bool.false_eq_true, Matrix.conjTranspose_add, add_sub_add_left_eq_sub]
   360	+  have hminusStar :

   381	+/-- The state-dependent squared distance between binary observables in terms
   382	+of their correlation. -/
   383	+theorem stateDepDistSq_eq_two_sub_two_mul_correlation
   384	+    {ι : Type} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
   385	+    (S T ρ : Op ι) (hS : IsBinaryObservable S)
   386	+    (hT : IsBinaryObservable T) (hρ : ρ.PosSemidef)
   387	+    (htrace : Matrix.trace ρ = 1) :
   388	+    stateDepDistSq S T ρ =
   389	+      2 - 2 * (Matrix.trace (S * T * ρ)).re := by
   390	+  have hstar :
   391	+      star (Matrix.trace (S * T * ρ)) = Matrix.trace (T * S * ρ) := by
   392	+    calc
   393	+      star (Matrix.trace (S * T * ρ)) = Matrix.trace ((S * T * ρ)ᴴ) := by
   394	+        rw [Matrix.trace_conjTranspose]
   395	+      _ = Matrix.trace (ρ * T * S) := by
   396	+        simp [Matrix.conjTranspose_mul, hS.1.eq, hT.1.eq, hρ.isHermitian.eq,
   397	+          Matrix.mul_assoc]
   398	+      _ = Matrix.trace (T * S * ρ) := by
   399	+        exact (Matrix.trace_mul_cycle T S ρ).symm
   400	+  have hcross :
   401	+      (Matrix.trace (S * T * ρ)).re = (Matrix.trace (T * S * ρ)).re := by
   402	+    have := congrArg Complex.re hstar
   403	+    simpa [Complex.star_def, Complex.conj_re] using this
   404	+  have hdiff :
   405	+      (S - T)ᴴ * (S - T) =
   406	+        (2 : ℂ) • (1 : Op ι) - S * T - T * S := by
   407	+    rw [Matrix.conjTranspose_sub, hS.1.eq, hT.1.eq]
   408	+    calc
   409	+      (S - T) * (S - T) = S * S - S * T - T * S + T * T := by
   410	+        noncomm_ring
   411	+      _ = (2 : ℂ) • (1 : Op ι) - S * T - T * S := by
   412	+        rw [hS.2, hT.2]
   413	+        module
   414	+  unfold stateDepDistSq
   415	+  rw [hdiff]
   416	+  simp only [Matrix.sub_mul, Matrix.trace_sub, Complex.sub_re]
   417	+  rw [smul_mul_assoc, one_mul, Matrix.trace_smul, htrace]
   418	+  norm_num [Complex.mul_re]
   419	+  rw [hcross]
   420	+  ring

   655	+\section{At a glance}
   656	+
   657	+\begin{itemize}
   658	+  \item \textbf{Difficulty.} Medium.  The factor-of-two calculation is
   659	+  elementary, but the counterexample must remain valid after the ancillary
   660	+  extension allowed by the theorem.
   661	+  \item \textbf{Estimated weight.} The formal adapter consists of one binary
   662	+  effect definition and two distance identities, requiring roughly 70--100
   663	+  lines of matrix algebra.  Correcting the source-facing theorem is a separate
   664	+  statement-realignment task.
   665	+  \item \textbf{Mathlib/project split.} About 60\% is direct finite-matrix and
   666	+  finite-sum algebra; the remaining 40\% is the project-local Boolean Fourier
   667	+  and state-dependent distance interface.
   668	+  \item \textbf{Key Mathlib inputs.} Finite sums on the Boolean cube, complex
   669	+  matrices and conjugate transpose, cyclicity of trace, and simultaneous
   670	+  spectral decomposition for commuting Hermitian matrices.
   671	+\end{itemize}

   673	+\section{Key theorem forms}
   674	+
   675	+Let $S$ and $T$ be binary observables and let $\rho$ be a positive
   676	+semidefinite operator of trace one.  We distinguish the state-dependent
   677	+operator distance from the distance between their associated binary projective
   678	+measurements:
   679	+\begin{align*}
   680	+  d_\rho(S,T)^2
   681	+    &:= \Re\tr\big((S-T)^\dagger(S-T)\rho\big), \\
   682	+  \dbin_\rho(S,T)^2
   683	+    &:= \sum_{s\in\{+,-\}}
   684	+      \Re\tr\big((P_S^s-P_T^s)^\dagger
   685	+                       (P_S^s-P_T^s)\rho\big),
   686	+  \qquad P_S^\pm := \frac{\Id\pm S}{2}.
   687	+\end{align*}
   688	+The normalization and correlation identities are
   689	+\begin{align}
   690	+  \dbin_\rho(S,T)^2 &= \frac12 d_\rho(S,T)^2,
   691	+    \tag{normalization}\label{eq:normalization}\\
   692	+  d_\rho(S,T)^2
   693	+    &= 2-2\Re\tr(ST\rho),
   694	+    \tag{operator correlation}\label{eq:operator-correlation}\\
   695	+  \dbin_\rho(S,T)^2
   696	+    &= 1-\Re\tr(ST\rho).
   697	+    \tag{binary correlation}\label{eq:binary-correlation}
   698	+\end{align}
   699	+Consequently, the conclusion delivered by the quantum linearity argument can
   700	+be written either as
   701	+\[
   702	+  \mathbb E_a\dbin_{\rho'}(\mathcal A(a),A(a))^2\leq\delta
   703	+\]
   704	+or, equivalently, as
   705	+\[
   706	+  \mathbb E_a d_{\rho'}(\mathcal A(a),A(a))^2\leq2\delta.
   707	+\]
   708	+These are not equivalent to the same bound $\delta$ for the mean squared
   709	+state-dependent operator distance.%
   710	+\footnote{The formal declarations are \leanid{binaryObservableEffect},
   711	+\leanid{binaryObservableDistSq},
   712	+\leanid{binaryObservableDistSq\_eq\_stateDepDistSq\_div\_two},
   713	+\leanid{stateDepDistSq\_eq\_two\_sub\_two\_mul\_correlation}, and
   714	+\leanid{binaryObservableDistSq\_eq\_one\_sub\_correlation} in
   715	+\doclink{MIPStarRE/QPBT/Combining/Linearity/BooleanFourier.lean}.}
   716	+
   717	+\section{The source calculation}
   718	+
   719	+Natarajan and Vidick define the distance between two POVMs by summing the
   720	+squared state-dependent distances between corresponding square roots
   721	+\cite[Section~3.1]{Natarajan2017Linearity}.  For projective measurements the
   722	+square roots are the effects themselves.  In the binary case their calculation
   723	+expands $P_S^\pm=(\Id\pm S)/2$ and obtains
   724	+\[
   725	+  \dbin_\rho(S,T)^2
   726	+    = 1-\frac12\tr_\rho(ST+TS)
   727	+    = \frac12\tr_\rho((S-T)^2).
   728	+  \tag{source equation (3)}
   729	+\]
   730	+This is equation~(3) at lines~903--910 of the in-repository source mirror.%
   731	+\footnote{See
   732	+\path{references/nv-paper/fullpaper.tex}, lines~866--912.  The quantum
   733	+linearity theorem and its Fourier--Naimark proof are at lines~1074--1112.}
   734	+The next line identifies the final expression with the squared state-dependent
   735	+operator distance.  The operator-distance definition at lines~873--875 is
   736	+printed with $\rho$ occurring twice,
   737	+\[
   738	+  d_\rho(S,T)^2 = \tr_\rho\big((S-T)^\dagger(S-T)\rho\big),
   739	+  \qquad \tr_\rho(X) := \tr(\rho X),
   740	+\]
   741	+and we read the duplication as typographical, keeping the single $\rho$ of the
   742	+definition of $d$ above.  Under that reading the squared state-dependent
   743	+operator distance is $\tr_\rho((S-T)^2)$ rather than one half of that
   744	+quantity.  Thus the calculation through line~910 is correct and the equality
   745	+on line~911 loses a factor of two.
   746	+
   747	+The Fourier--Naimark proof is consistent with the measurement normalization.
   748	+It proves
   749	+\[
   750	+  \mathbb E_a\operatorname{CON}_{\rho'}(A(a),\mathcal A(a))
   751	+  = \frac12+\frac12\mathbb E_{a,b}
   752	+       \tr_\rho(A(a)A(b)A(a+b)).
   753	+\]
   754	+The hypothesis therefore makes the consistency deficit at most $\delta/2$.
   755	+For binary projective measurements, the squared measurement distance is twice
   756	+that deficit, giving the bound $\delta$ for the squared binary-measurement
   757	+distance and the bound $2\delta$ for the squared state-dependent operator
   758	+distance.

   760	+\section{A four-point counterexample}
   761	+
   762	+The bound $\delta$ for the mean squared state-dependent operator distance is
   763	+false.  Let $G=(\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z)^2$, choose $r\in G\setminus\{0\}$, take
   764	+the one-dimensional state $\rho=1$, and define scalar binary observables by
   765	+\[
   766	+  A(a)=\begin{cases}
   767	+    -1,&a=r,\\
   768	+     1,&a\neq r.
   769	+  \end{cases}
   770	+\]
   771	+For the characters $\chi_u(a)=(-1)^{u\cdot a}$, the normalized Fourier
   772	+coefficients satisfy
   773	+\[
   774	+  \widehat A(0)=\frac12,
   775	+  \qquad
   776	+  \widehat A(u)=-\frac12\chi_u(r)\quad(u\neq0).
   777	+\]
   778	+Their multiset is
   779	+$\{\frac12,\frac12,\frac12,-\frac12\}$, and hence
   780	+\[
   781	+  \mathbb E_{a,b}A(a)A(b)A(a+b)
   782	+    =\sum_u\widehat A(u)^3=\frac14.
   783	+\]
   784	+The correlation hypothesis therefore holds with $\delta=3/4$.
   785	+
   786	+Every scalar exact Boolean representation is one of the characters $\chi_u$,
   787	+and its mean squared state-dependent operator distance from $A$ is
   788	+\[
   789	+  \mathbb E_a |A(a)-\chi_u(a)|^2
   790	+    =2-2\widehat A(u)\geq1.
   791	+\]
   792	+Allowing an ancillary space does not reduce this lower bound.  Exact linearity
   793	+and the binary-observable relations make the operators $\mathcal A(a)$ a
   794	+commuting family of Hermitian involutions.  Their simultaneous spectral
   795	+subspaces carry characters of $G$.  Evaluation in any density operator is
   796	+therefore a convex combination of the scalar character correlations above, so
   797	+the mean squared state-dependent operator distance remains at least $1$.  It
   798	+cannot be at most $\delta=3/4$.  By~\eqref{eq:normalization}, the corresponding
   799	+mean squared binary-measurement distance has lower bound $1/2$, which is
   800	+compatible with the provider's conclusion.

   802	+\section{Comparison with the blueprint and formalization}
   803	+
   804	+The QPBT paper quotes the quantum linearity theorem at lines~711--725 of its
   805	+Pauli-basis analysis and defers its proof to Natarajan and Vidick.%

   369	    (htrace : Matrix.trace ρ = 1) :
   370	    stateDepDistSq S T ρ =
   371	      2 - 2 * (Matrix.trace (S * T * ρ)).re := by
   372	  have hstar :
   373	      star (Matrix.trace (S * T * ρ)) = Matrix.trace (T * S * ρ) := by
   374	    calc
   375	      star (Matrix.trace (S * T * ρ)) = Matrix.trace ((S * T * ρ)ᴴ) := by
   376	        rw [Matrix.trace_conjTranspose]
   377	      _ = Matrix.trace (ρ * T * S) := by
   378	        simp [Matrix.conjTranspose_mul, hS.1.eq, hT.1.eq, hρ.isHermitian.eq,
   379	          Matrix.mul_assoc]
   380	      _ = Matrix.trace (T * S * ρ) := by
   381	        exact (Matrix.trace_mul_cycle T S ρ).symm
   382	  have hcross :
   383	      (Matrix.trace (S * T * ρ)).re = (Matrix.trace (T * S * ρ)).re := by
   384	    have := congrArg Complex.re hstar
   385	    simpa [Complex.star_def, Complex.conj_re] using this
   386	  have hdiff :
   387	      (S - T)ᴴ * (S - T) =
   388	        (2 : ℂ) • (1 : Op ι) - S * T - T * S := by
   389	    rw [Matrix.conjTranspose_sub, hS.1.eq, hT.1.eq]
   390	    calc
   391	      (S - T) * (S - T) = S * S - S * T - T * S + T * T := by
   392	        noncomm_ring
   393	      _ = (2 : ℂ) • (1 : Op ι) - S * T - T * S := by
   394	        rw [hS.2, hT.2]
   395	        module
   396	  unfold stateDepDistSq
   397	  rw [hdiff]
   398	  simp only [Matrix.sub_mul, Matrix.trace_sub, Complex.sub_re]
   399	  rw [smul_mul_assoc, one_mul, Matrix.trace_smul, htrace]
   400	  norm_num [Complex.mul_re]
   401	  rw [hcross]
   402	  ring
   403	
   404	/-- The squared binary-measurement distance is one minus the real
   405	state-dependent correlation. -/
   406	theorem binaryObservableDistSq_eq_one_sub_correlation
   407	    {ι : Type} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
   408	    (S T ρ : Op ι) (hS : IsBinaryObservable S)
   409	    (hT : IsBinaryObservable T) (hρ : ρ.PosSemidef)
   410	    (htrace : Matrix.trace ρ = 1) :
   411	    binaryObservableDistSq S T ρ =
   412	      1 - (Matrix.trace (S * T * ρ)).re := by
   413	  rw [binaryObservableDistSq_eq_stateDepDistSq_div_two,
   414	    stateDepDistSq_eq_two_sub_two_mul_correlation S T ρ hS hT hρ htrace]
   415	  ring
   416	
   417	end

    34	def IsBinaryObservable {ι : Type} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
    35	    (O : Op ι) : Prop :=

    38	/-- The rank-one density operator associated with an ancillary vector. -/

    40	    (v : EuclideanSpace ℂ ι) : Op ι :=
    41	  let w := (EuclideanSpace.equiv ι ℂ) v

    47	noncomputable def stateDepDistSq {ι : Type} [Fintype ι]
    48	    (S T ρ : Op ι) : ℝ :=

    52	
    53	The statement is `thm:linearity` in

    59	provider-faithful form imposes no upper bound on `δ`, preserves the error,
    60	asserts exact linearity for every pair, and averages closeness only over `u`.
    61	The paper quotation instead adds `δ ≤ 1`, phrases closeness pointwise under a
    62	pair quantifier, and appends `L 0 = 1`; those three deviations are not

    65	theorem exists_exactly_linear_observables {ι : Type}
    66	    [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
    67	    (t : ℕ) (ht : 0 < t) (δ : ℝ) (hδ : 0 ≤ δ)
    68	    (ρ : Op ι) (hρ : ρ.PosSemidef) (htrace : ρ.trace = 1)
    69	    (O : (Fin t → ZMod 2) → Op ι)
    70	    (hO : ∀ u, IsBinaryObservable (O u))
    71	    (hcorrelation :
    72	      1 - δ ≤ avgOver
    73	        (uniformDistribution
    74	          ((Fin t → ZMod 2) × (Fin t → ZMod 2)))
    75	        (fun pair =>
    76	          (Matrix.trace
    77	            (O pair.1 * O pair.2 * O (pair.1 + pair.2) * ρ)).re)) :
    78	    ∃ (ι' : Type) (_ : Fintype ι') (_ : DecidableEq ι')
    79	        (anc : EuclideanSpace ℂ ι'),
    80	      ‖anc‖ = 1 ∧
    81	        ∃ L : (Fin t → ZMod 2) → Op (ι × ι'),
    82	          (∀ u, IsBinaryObservable (L u)) ∧
    83	          (∀ u u', L u * L u' = L (u + u')) ∧
    84	          avgOver (uniformDistribution (Fin t → ZMod 2))
    85	              (fun u => stateDepDistSq (L u)
    86	                (heteroKron (O u) (1 : Op ι'))

85	% to O^u on average over uniformly random u only, in mean squared
    86	% state-dependent distance with the error delta preserved; it is stated for
    87	% an arbitrary density operator rho on a single Hilbert space, with the
    88	% index group written {0,1}^n under bitwise XOR (here F_2^t, additively) and
    89	% Obs(H) denoting the Hermitian unitaries, i.e. the binary observables of
    90	% def:povm-conventions. In the closeness conclusion an operator on H is
    91	% compared with an operator on the extension via its ampliation S ot Id. The
    92	% mirror's quotation
    93	% (references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:713-725)
    94	% inserts the restriction 0 <= delta <= 1, places the closeness conclusion,
    95	% together with the exact linearity, under the quantifier "for all u, u' in
    96	% F_2^t", and appends "L^u = Id when u = 0"; none of these is part of the
    97	% cited theorem, and none is reproduced here. See rem:linearity-import.
    98	\begin{theorem}[Quantum linearity test~\cite{Natarajan2017Linearity}]
    99		\label{thm:linearity}
   100		\lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.IsBinaryObservable, MIPStarRE.QPBT.stateDepDistSq}
   101		\lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.exists_exactly_linear_observables}
   102		\notready
   103		\uses{def:povm-conventions}
   104		Let $t$ be a positive integer and $\delta \ge 0$. Let $\rho$ be a
   105		density operator on a Hilbert space $\hilb$ and let
   106		$\{\mathcal{O}^u\}$ be a set of binary observables indexed by
   107		$u \in \F_2^t$ acting on $\hilb$, such that on average over $u, u'$
   108		chosen uniformly at random from $\F_2^t$,
   109		\[
   110			\E_{u,u'} \Tr\big(\mathcal{O}^u \, \mathcal{O}^{u'} \,
   111			\mathcal{O}^{u+u'} \, \rho\big) \ge 1 - \delta\,.
   112		\]
   113		Then there exist a Hilbert space $\hilb'$, a pure state
   114		$\ket{\mathrm{anc}} \in \hilb'$, and binary observables
   115		$\{\mathcal{L}^u\}$ indexed by $u \in \F_2^t$ acting on
   116		$\hilb \ot \hilb'$ such that, writing
   117		$\rho' = \rho \ot \ket{\mathrm{anc}}\bra{\mathrm{anc}}$, the exact
   118		linearity
   119		\[
   120			\mathcal{L}^u \, \mathcal{L}^{u'} = \mathcal{L}^{u+u'}
   121		\]
   122		holds for all $u, u' \in \F_2^t$, and
   123		\[
   124			\E_{u} \, d_{\rho'}\big(\mathcal{L}^u,\ \mathcal{O}^u \ot
   125			\Id_{\hilb'}\big)^2 \le \delta\,,
   126		\]
   127		where the expectation is over $u$ chosen uniformly at random from
   128		$\F_2^t$ and
   129		$d_{\sigma}(S,T)
   130		= \big(\Tr\big((S-T)^\dagger (S-T)\, \sigma\big)\big)^{1/2}$
   131		denotes the state-dependent distance with respect to a density
   132		operator $\sigma$.
   133	\end{theorem}
   134	\begin{proof}
   135		This is Theorem~10 of Natarajan and
   136		Vidick~\cite{Natarajan2017Linearity}, imported as an external result;
   137		no proof is given in \cite{Ji2020MIPStar}, which invokes the result
   138		directly. The verification obligations attached to the import at its
   139		point of use --- the correspondence between the correlation hypothesis
   140		above and the relation $\approx_\delta$ of
   141		Definition~\ref{def:povm-distance}, the instantiation of $\rho$ as a
   142		reduced state of $\ket{\hat\psi}$, the absorption of the ancilla
   143		register into padding of the strategy state, and the identity
   144		$\mathcal{L}^0 = \Id$ --- are enumerated in
   145		Remark~\ref{rem:linearity-import} and addressed in the proof of
   146		Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-4-10}.
   147	\end{proof}
   148	
   149	\begin{remark}[Obligations of the linearity-theorem import]
   150		\label{rem:linearity-import}
   151		Theorem~\ref{thm:linearity} is stated in the form proved in
   152		\cite{Natarajan2017Linearity}. Three features are load-bearing for the
   153		proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-4-10}: the error is preserved without
   154		polynomial loss ($\delta$ in the hypothesis becomes $\delta$ in the
   155		conclusion); the linearity of the $\{\mathcal{L}^u\}$ is exact and
   156		holds for all pairs $(u,u')$, not merely on average; and the
   157		hypothesis carries no upper bound on $\delta$, so the theorem may be
   158		applied separately for each pair $(x,z)$ with hypothesis error the
   159		conditional linearity defect given $(x,z)$, a quantity for which no a
   160		priori bound is available. The closeness of $\mathcal{L}^u$ to
   161		$\mathcal{O}^u$ is guaranteed on average over a uniformly random $u$
   162		only; this averaged form suffices because the $\mathcal{L}^u$ enter
   163		the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-4-10} only through averages over $u$.
   164		The quotation of the theorem in \cite{Ji2020MIPStar} differs from the
   165		cited statement in three respects: it inserts the restriction
   166		$0 \le \delta \le 1$, which would block the fiberwise application
   167		just described; it places the closeness conclusion, together with the
   168		exact linearity, under the quantifier ``for all $u, u' \in \F_2^t$'',
   169		a strengthening of the theorem proved in
   170		\cite{Natarajan2017Linearity}; and it appends the identity
   171		$\mathcal{L}^u = \Id$ for $u = 0$. None of the three is reproduced
   172		here: the restriction is dropped, the pointwise closeness is not
   173		used, and the appended identity is instead derived from the
   174		conclusion, since exact linearity at $u = u' = 0$ gives
   175		$(\mathcal{L}^0)^2 = \mathcal{L}^0$, and an idempotent unitary equals
   176		the identity. The import carries two conversion obligations,
   177		discharged in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-4-10}: the theorem is
   178		instantiated with $\rho$ the reduced density operator of
   179		$\ket{\hat\psi}$ on the registers carrying the observables, so that
   180		traces against $\rho$ are expectation values in $\ket{\hat\psi}$; and
   181		the correlation hypothesis and the squared-distance conclusion are
   182		converted to and from the relation $\approx_\delta$ of
   183		Definition~\ref{def:povm-distance} by expanding the square, using
   184		unitarity of the observables, and relabelling the averaged index
   185		pair, at the cost of the constant factors absorbed by that
   186		definition. One obligation remains open and is flagged where it
   187		arises: the ancilla register $\hilb'$ and its state
   188		$\ket{\mathrm{anc}}$ produced by the theorem, which may depend on the
   189		pair $(x,z)$, must be absorbed --- uniformly in $(x,z)$ --- into
   190		zero-state padding of the strategy state, padding that the source
   191		assumes present without construction.
   192	\end{remark}
   193	
   194	\begin{remark}[Normalization of the distance in the linearity conclusion]
   195		\label{rem:linearity-distance-normalization}
   196		The conclusion of Theorem~\ref{thm:linearity} bounds the mean squared
   197		state-dependent operator distance
   198		$\E_u \, d_{\rho'}(\mathcal{L}^u, \mathcal{O}^u \ot \Id_{\hilb'})^2$ by
   199		$\delta$, as quoted in \cite{Ji2020MIPStar}. The calculation behind that
   200		bound in \cite[Section~3.1]{Natarajan2017Linearity} computes the squared
   201		distance between the binary projective measurements associated with the
   202		observables, which is half the squared operator distance, and then
   203		identifies the two quantities; the identification loses that factor. What
   204		the Fourier argument proves is the bound $\delta$ for the mean squared
   205		measurement distance, equivalently $2\delta$ for the mean squared operator
   206		distance, and the bound $\delta$ for the mean squared operator distance
   207		stated above is refuted by a four-point counterexample
   208		\cite{gap:qpbt_linearity-distance-normalization}. The normalization
   209		identities are recorded in Lemma~\ref{lem:binary-measurement-distance}.
   210		Thus the displayed bound in Theorem~\ref{thm:linearity} is not the
   211		conclusion established by the Fourier argument.
   212	\end{remark}

   920	
   921	  Likewise, if $\{C_a\}$ a family of operators such that $\|\sum_a C_aC_a^\dagger\|\leq K$ and $\{M^a\}$

    17	\section{Purpose}
    18	
    19	When a formalization relies on a cited mathematical source, the cited source
    20	should remain intact.  It is a source, not an errata file.  If a possible gap,
    21	missing hypothesis, incorrect numerical constant, or other mathematical
    22	discrepancy is found, the matter should be recorded in a separate LaTeX note.
    23	In this repository such notes live under \path{docs/paper-gaps/}.  The same
    24	principle applies when the formal development has already diverged from the
    25	cited source, for instance by changing a statement so that it compiles, or by
    26	using a different mathematical route because an available formal-library theorem
    27	has a slightly different form.  Such a note is a mathematical note first, and a
    28	record of the formalization second: it should be readable by a mathematician or
    29	mathematical physicist who has not followed the issue discussion.
    30	
    31	The note should isolate the mathematical mechanism.  It should say what the
    32	cited source asserts, what the cited results actually imply, where a term or
    33	hypothesis is lost, and what statement the formal development proves instead.
    34	If the formal proof takes a different route, the note should explain the
    35	replacement argument and the hypotheses on which it rests.  This is especially
    36	important when the proof uses a theorem, construction, or convention from
    37	Mathlib which is not part of the cited argument.  In that case the note should
    38	state the Mathlib result in ordinary mathematical language, explain how it is
    39	specialized to the notation of the paper, and compare its hypotheses and
    40	conclusion with the step it replaces.  It should not merely say that \Lean{} did
    41	not accept a proof, that the modified proof compiles, or that a named library
    42	lemma was applied.
    43	
    44	The documents in this directory should themselves follow this standard.  A
    45	policy or template which reads like a checklist will tend to produce checklist
    46	notes; the examples and templates should therefore be written as mathematical
    47	prose.
    48	
    49	\section{Concision and Readability}
    50	
    51	A paper-gap note should be short enough that a reader can understand the issue
    52	in one sitting.  The first page should answer four questions: what the source
    53	uses, how hard the remaining formal work is, what the formalization or audit
    54	checked, and what the current verdict is.  Begin with a short
    55	\emph{At a glance} section when the note concerns an open or recently resolved
    56	formalization task.  That section should estimate the difficulty, the rough
    57	implementation weight, the split between Mathlib reuse and project-local work,
    58	and the key Mathlib APIs or modules.  Use honest ranges, not false precision.
    59	
    60	The \emph{Key theorem forms} section should be Section~2, immediately after
    61	\emph{At a glance}.  Put the theorem forms before the source details so the
    62	reader knows what the formalization is aiming to prove.  After that, keep the
    63	source assertion, the mechanism being checked, the blueprint/formal comparison,
    64	and the conclusion.  Use more sections only when a counterexample or long
    65	derivation genuinely needs room.
    66	
    67	Keep background to the minimum needed for the local point.  Prefer one clear
    68	special case over a general restatement of the surrounding theorem.  Use displayed
    69	equations for the source assertion, the key calculation, and the theorem forms;
    70	avoid displays for traceability data, declaration names, or long lists.  The
    71	blueprint/formal comparison should be compact and should not repeat the theorem
    72	forms.  The section ``Form of the Note'' below specifies where traceability data
    73	belongs; the body should read as mathematical prose, not as a log.
    74	
    75	If the verdict is that there is no mathematical discrepancy, say so plainly and
    76	stop.  Keep the conclusion highly compact, normally under twenty source lines.
    77	If the only remaining work is an implementation task, name it briefly and link
    78	the issue or pull request in a footnote.
    79	
    80	\section{When the Investigation Starts}
    81	
    82	The investigation starts when the obstruction appears to be mathematical rather
    83	than merely formal.  No final judgement is needed at this stage.  It is enough
    84	that, after reading the relevant source and attempting the corresponding formal
    85	statement, the proof seems to require a different scalar, an additional
    86	hypothesis, a different tensor placement, a distinction between two objects which
    87	the prose identifies, or an auxiliary assertion not supplied by the cited
    88	argument.
    89	
    90	The same investigation should also start when such a deviation is discovered
    91	after the fact.  If the existing formal development or informal blueprint has
    92	already changed the statement, strengthened a hypothesis, weakened a conclusion,
    93	inserted an unadvertised lemma, or replaced the cited proof by a different
    94	formal-library argument, the mathematical change should be documented even if all
    95	relevant files already compile.
    96	
    97	At this early stage the purpose is to preserve the question while it is still
    98	local.  The note may later conclude that the matter is only notational, that an
    99	intermediate estimate in the cited source needs a harmless correction, that a
   100	missing hypothesis is genuinely needed, or that no discrepancy remains.  Thus
   101	the trigger is not the severity of the eventual verdict, but the appearance of a
   102	real mismatch between the cited reasoning and the statement that can be
   103	formalized.
   104	
   105	A failed tactic search, a missing formal lemma, or an inconvenient coercion is
   106	not enough.  The obstruction must survive translation back into ordinary
   107	mathematics.
   108	
   109	Sometimes an investigation uncovers an improvement that is not a discrepancy:
   110	the formalization works correctly, but it could be simplified by using an
   111	existing library, replacing a custom type, or adopting a cleaner proof route.
   112	These are not, by themselves, paper-gap notes.  They are action items.  When
   113	such an improvement is identified, open a GitHub issue or pull request that
   114	describes the proposed change.  If the investigation also produces a paper-gap
   115	note, link the issue or pull request from that note: the note records the
   116	mathematical justification, and the issue or pull request drives the
   117	implementation.
   118	
   119	\section{When to Write a Note}
   120	
   121	A note should be written once the source argument and the formal proof no longer
   122	match as mathematical arguments.  This includes, for instance, a numerical
   123	estimate whose constant does not follow from the cited lemma, a displayed
   124	conclusion which uses an unstated hypothesis, or a step in which two objects are
   125	identified although they must remain distinct.  In analytic, algebraic,
   126	probabilistic, or quantum arguments, such distinctions may concern the domain of
   127	a map, the placement of a tensor factor, the type of an outcome, the distinction
   128	between a structure and a substructure, or the scalar carried by an approximation
   129	relation.
   130	
   131	A note is required when an audit finds that a Lean declaration associated with a
   132	source-labelled statement has acquired an extra non-source hypothesis, such as
   133	bridge, residual, repair, producer, or obligation-structure data.  Such a
   134	declaration is temporary proof debt, not a replacement for the source theorem,
   135	and should not be introduced merely to avoid a \verb|sorry|.  The note must say
   136	plainly that the Lean result is conditional, identify the source-faithful theorem
   137	form that remains to be proved, and give the intended obligation discharger or
   138	removal plan.  The blueprint should not mark the source-labelled statement with
   139	\verb|\leanok| by pointing to this conditional helper.
   140	
   141	Changing a Lean theorem away from the statement in
   142	\path{references/ldt-paper/} is strongly discouraged.  A paper-gap note should
   143	not make such a change look routine: it should explain the mathematical
   144	necessity, or else classify the change as proof debt to be removed.
   145	
   146	When an existing conditional helper is audited, the first task is to extract any
   147	argument it already contains into source-faithful lemmas.  If the remaining
   148	bridge hypothesis cannot be derived from the paper hypotheses, the formal
   149	development should restore the source theorem statement and record the missing
   150	proof obligation explicitly, rather than retaining the strengthened statement as
   151	though it were the paper theorem.
   152	
   153	This requirement is not meant to classify every explicit Lean side condition as
   154	a discrepancy.  Positivity, nonemptiness, decidability, field-model instances,
   155	and denominator nonvanishing hypotheses may be faithful encodings of the domain
   156	in which the paper's theorem is stated.  The note should distinguish such
   157	boundary hypotheses from hypotheses that supply an unproved step of the paper
   158	argument.
   159	
   160	A note is also appropriate when the proof becomes formal only after changing an
   161	intermediate scalar, weakening a conclusion, strengthening a hypothesis, or
   162	inserting an additional lemma which is not simply an expansion of the cited
   163	argument.  These are mathematical changes, even when they are harmless for the
   164	final theorem.  It is likewise appropriate when an available formal-library
   165	theorem proves the needed result under a somewhat different formulation from the
   166	cited source.  In that case the note should be deliberately pedagogical.  It
   167	should explain, in ordinary mathematical language, what the replacement result
   168	says, how it is specialized, which hypotheses are new or differently packaged,
   169	and why the resulting statement is a legitimate substitute for the step in the
   170	cited argument.  If the issue remains open after reasonable attempts, the note
   171	should say what has been checked and what remains unknown.
   172	
   173	\section{Counterexamples}
   174	
   175	If the cited assertion appears to be false, the note should not stop at saying
   176	that the proof cannot be formalized.  It should give the counterexample, or the
   177	smallest relevant part of it, in ordinary mathematical notation.  The example
   178	should be accompanied by enough verification that the reader can see both sides:
   179	the hypotheses of the cited assertion hold, and its conclusion fails.
   180	
   181	When feasible, the counterexample should also be formalized in \Lean{}.  This is
   182	especially valuable when the example is finite, algebraic, computational, or
   183	otherwise small enough that the failure can be checked without reproducing the
   184	whole surrounding theory.  The note should then state the mathematical content
   185	of the checked counterexample and identify the corresponding Lean declaration in
   186	a footnote.  The Lean file is not a substitute for the prose: the prose should
   187	still explain why the example refutes the cited assertion.
   188	
   189	\section{Revision of a Note}
   190	
   191	A paper-gap note may be provisional.  It may begin as soon as the mathematical
   192	obstruction has been isolated well enough to state the question, and it may be
   193	revised as the calculation, the blueprint, or the corresponding \Lean{}
   194	declarations become clearer.  The first version need not know the final
   195	classification, but it should say plainly which mathematical point is known and
   196	which point remains unsettled.
   197	
   198	Later revisions should not make the note into a chronological log.  They should
   199	rewrite the document so that it remains a coherent account of the present
   200	mathematical understanding.  If the verdict changes, the conclusion should state
   201	the current verdict; the linked issue or pull request can preserve the earlier
   202	discussion.
   203	
   204	\section{Form of the Note}
   205	
   206	Each note should stand on its own.  It should give the date, cite the relevant
   207	source article, and provide enough traceability for the reader to locate the
   208	original passage and the project discussion.  GitHub issues and pull requests may
   209	be linked with \verb|\href|, and source files, line ranges, and labels should be
   210	recorded when they help the reader check the claim.  These references should
   211	serve the exposition rather than govern it: the main text should be organized
   212	around the mathematical assertion and its proof.
   213	
   214	The note should introduce its notation before using it.  Symbols for
   215	measurements, tensor factors, approximation relations, and error parameters
   216	should be named in prose.  If an approximation relation is state-dependent, the
   217	state should be named, or its defining expression should be given when this can
   218	be done briefly.  Only after the notation is in place should the note state the
   219	assertion in the cited source, using a bibliographic citation such as
   220	\verb|\cite[Section~...]{...}| when the section or chapter is known.
   221	
   222	Only the relevant hypotheses should be reproduced.  If the question is a scalar
   223	substitution, a missing term, or a missing hypothesis, the note should not quote
   224	a long unrelated part of the proof.  It should give the cited lemma or
   225	proposition in the special case actually used, then display the calculation or
   226	logical implication in which the discrepancy appears.
   227	
   228	Displayed equations should be used with restraint.  They are appropriate for the
   229	source estimate being checked, the cited estimate in the form actually used, and
   230	the calculation where a term or hypothesis appears or disappears.  When a
   231	displayed equation is identified by a source label, the label should appear on
   232	the right of the display, while the surrounding prose refers to the mathematical
   233	assertion itself.  The standard \texttt{amsmath} command \verb|\tag| is the
   234	right mechanism for this; a separate local convention should be introduced only
   235	if the standard mechanism is genuinely insufficient.  For a multi-line aligned
   236	display, tag the individual lines that carry the source information rather than
   237	forcing a long combined label below the equations.  Short
   238	scalar definitions and elementary inequalities should remain inline when the
   239	sentence reads better that way.  As in ordinary mathematical writing, a displayed
   240	formula is part of the surrounding sentence and should be punctuated accordingly.
   241	
   242	Bibliographic entries used only by these notes should live in
   243	\path{docs/paper-gaps/references.bib}.  A new note should ordinarily begin from
   244	\path{docs/paper-gaps/template.tex}, which records the common LaTeX preamble,
   245	the local bibliography, and a model for right-hand source labels in displayed
   246	equations.
   247	
   248	Blueprint prose cites a note like any other source, with
   249	\verb|\cite{gap:<slug>}|; the bibliography entry in
   250	\path{blueprint/src/references.bib} carries the published URL of the note,
   251	whether the note lives in this repository or in another one.  Lean docstrings
   252	and comments use the repository path form \path{docs/paper-gaps/<slug>.tex}.
   253	
   254	The note should then compare the cited source with the informal blueprint, if
   255	there is one, and with the formal statement.  This comparison should be written
   256	in ordinary mathematical prose.  Formal declaration names and source paths should
   257	be supplied only to identify the exact formal statements, and normally belong in
   258	footnotes.
   259	
   260	The conclusion should give a verdict.  It may say that there is no discrepancy,

    17	\section{Purpose}
    18	
    19	This note fixes terminology for a recurring failure mode in the formalization
    20	of the low individual degree test paper, \path{arXiv:2009.12982}.  It
    21	complements the note-writing policy in \path{docs/paper-gaps/policy.tex} and
    22	the source-statement audit tracked historically in \ghissue{1458}.  The current
    23	source-boundary proof holes are tracked in \ghissue{1507} and \ghissue{422}.
    24	A proof may be blocked at
    25	an intermediate mathematical assertion.  If that assertion is added as a new
    26	hypothesis to a theorem labelled as a paper theorem, the resulting \Lean{}
    27	theorem
    28	may be correct as a conditional statement, but it is no longer the theorem in
    29	the cited source.  The apparent proof has not closed the paper theorem; it has
    30	moved a proof obligation into the theorem statement.
    31	
    32	The protocol below distinguishes such proof debt from legitimate formal
    33	boundary conditions and from genuine mathematical corrections.  It is meant for
    34	contributors and reviewers who must decide whether a bridge, residual, repair,
    35	input, or obligation structure is a proved local construction, a tracked proof
    36	gap, or statement drift which must be repaired before a theorem may be
    37	advertised as a source theorem.  The default rule is restrictive: such data
    38	must not be added to a paper-facing theorem unless it is part of the cited
    39	source statement or a documented faithful encoding of its ambient hypotheses.
    40	
    41	\section{Basic objects}
    42	
    43	\paragraph{Source theorem.}
    44	A source theorem is a theorem, lemma, proposition, or corollary in the paper
    45	source under \path{references/ldt-paper/}.  Its hypotheses and conclusion are
    46	the mathematical ground truth, subject only to faithful formal encoding and to
    47	documented paper-gap corrections.
    48	
    49	\paragraph{Paper-facing declaration.}
    50	A \Lean{} declaration is paper-facing when it is named or cited as the
    51	formalization of a source theorem, for instance through a blueprint
    52	\verb|\lean{}| link on a theorem environment carrying a paper label.  Such a
    53	declaration must match the source theorem in its public statement.  In
    54	particular, it may not add an unproved bridge, residual, repair, input,
    55	obligation structure, or other proof-obligation hypothesis which the paper does
    56	not assume.
    57	
    58	\paragraph{Proof obligation.}
    59	A proof obligation is an intermediate assertion needed by the proof of a source
    60	theorem.  It may be a construction, an estimate, a transport lemma, or a
    61	comparison between two formal representations.  If the paper proves or invokes
    62	this assertion, then the formalization should state it as a separate lemma or
    63	theorem and prove it from the upstream hypotheses.
    64	
    65	\paragraph{Obligation discharger.}
    66	An obligation discharger is a theorem or definition which constructs a proof
    67	obligation from the paper hypotheses already available at that point in the
    68	argument.  This is the preferred representation of missing work.  If the proof
    69	is not yet complete, the discharger may temporarily contain a tracked
    70	\verb|sorry|, but the paper-facing theorem should call it rather than assume
    71	its output as an additional theorem hypothesis.
    72	
    73	\paragraph{Conditional helper.}
    74	A conditional helper is a separately named theorem whose statement explicitly
    75	assumes a proof obligation.  Names such as
    76	\leanid{mainFormal\_ofInternalObligations},
    77	\leanid{orthonormalization\_ofInput}, or names whose suffix advertises the
    78	assumed obligation are permitted only when the declaration is not presented as
    79	the source theorem.  A conditional helper is a quarantine for downstream proof
    80	content; it does not close the source theorem.
    81	
    82	\section{Bridge, residual, repair, input, and obligation structures}
    83	
    84	The words \emph{bridge}, \emph{residual}, \emph{repair}, \emph{input}, and
    85	\emph{obligation structure} name possible formal shapes.  They become dangerous
    86	when their mathematical status is unclear or when their names make unproved
    87	data look like acceptable hypotheses of a source theorem.
    88	
    89	\paragraph{Bridge.}
    90	A bridge should be a transport theorem between two already defined
    91	mathematical forms: for example, a tensor-placement identity, a conversion
    92	between two equivalent consistency relations, or a statement translating a
    93	source object into a formal representation.  A bridge is harmless only after it
    94	is proved from previously available assumptions.  It becomes proof debt when it
    95	is assumed because the transport has not yet been proved.  It becomes theorem
    96	drift when the assumed bridge is added to a paper-facing theorem.
    97	
    98	\paragraph{Residual.}
    99	A residual is a named remainder after part of an argument has been performed.
   100	It is often a useful way to record the exact missing target after a completed
   101	construction.  A residual may appear as the conclusion of a helper theorem or
   102	as the input of a quarantined conditional helper.  It is not a permissible new
   103	assumption on a paper theorem unless the paper itself assumes that residual.
   104	
   105	\paragraph{Input.}
   106	An input is a named bundle of data or hypotheses consumed by a construction or
   107	conditional helper.  It is harmless only when each load-bearing field is either
   108	part of the source hypotheses or is produced by an earlier theorem.  It becomes
   109	proof debt when the bundle is merely assumed because the construction of its
   110	fields is missing.  It becomes theorem drift when such a bundle is added to the
   111	public statement of a source theorem.
   112	
   113	\paragraph{Repair.}
   114	A repair is a mathematical construction which replaces an approximate or
   115	partial object by a better object, usually with a quantitative estimate.  In
   116	the low individual degree test formalization, projectivization and
   117	orthonormalization repairs are genuine mathematical operations.  A repair
   118	should therefore appear as a construction or as a theorem discharging the
   119	corresponding obligation.  If a theorem assumes the output of the repair instead
   120	of constructing it, that theorem is conditional on the repair.
   121	
   122	\paragraph{Obligation structure.}
   123	An obligation structure is a record whose fields are the data and estimates
   124	needed by a later construction.  This is acceptable only as an internal target
   125	or as a hypothesis of a conditional helper.  Such a structure becomes statement
   126	drift if it is added to a paper-facing theorem instead of being constructed
   127	inside the proof.  The review question is whether every load-bearing field is
   128	proved from the source hypotheses or is explicitly tracked as a missing
   129	obligation.
   130	
   131	\section{The main failure mode}
   132	
   133	Suppose the paper proves
   134	\[
   135	  H \Longrightarrow C.
   136	\]
   137	During formalization, the proof may need an intermediate assertion \(B\).  The
   138	paper theorem should be represented as
   139	\[
   140	  H \Longrightarrow B \Longrightarrow C
   141	  \quad\text{inside the proof,}
   142	\]
   143	where \(B\) is obtained by a lemma or theorem from \(H\).  The following
   144	public statement is a different theorem:
   145	\[
   146	  H \land B \Longrightarrow C.
   147	\]
   148	It is not unsound in \Lean{}, but it is not the paper theorem.  It says that the
   149	conclusion follows if the missing bridge data is supplied.  Such a theorem is a
   150	conditional helper, even if its conclusion looks exactly like the paper's
   151	conclusion.
   152	
   153	This is the situation colloquially described as ``adding a bridge
   154	hypothesis''.  More precisely, an unproved intermediate step has been promoted
   155	from the proof body to the theorem's assumptions.  The correction is not to hide
   156	the hypothesis under a different structure name.  The correction is to keep a
   157	paper-facing theorem with the source statement and move the missing step to a
   158	named internal proof obligation.
   159	
   160	\section{Faithful boundary hypotheses}
   161	
   162	Not every extra formal hypothesis is a theorem drift.  Some hypotheses are
   163	faithful boundary conditions introduced by formal encoding.  Examples include
   164	nonnegativity needed for a real power, positivity needed to divide by a
   165	quantity, finiteness and nonemptiness of an index type, a field-model instance,
   166	or decidability instances required by \Lean{}.  Such hypotheses are acceptable
   167	when they express part of the mathematical ambient setting or make explicit a
   168	condition used implicitly in the paper.
   169	
   170	The distinction is load-bearing.  A faithful boundary hypothesis describes the
   171	domain in which the paper's objects live.  A proof-debt hypothesis supplies a
   172	mathematical step that the proof should derive.  If removing the hypothesis
   173	leaves an unproved construction or estimate from the paper proof, then the
   174	hypothesis is proof debt, not a boundary condition.
   175	
   176	\section{Definition drift and subtree repair}
   177	
   178	Definition drift is especially dangerous because it propagates.  If a
   179	definition is changed so that it no longer denotes the object in the paper,
   180	then every downstream theorem using that definition may continue to compile
   181	while proving statements about the wrong object.  Downstream theorem statements
   182	can then be repaired piecemeal, but the development remains unstable because
   183	the wrong definition is still upstream.
   184	
   185	When a definition mismatch is found, the repair should proceed by a subtree
   186	protocol.
   187	
   188	\begin{enumerate}
   189	  \item Identify the source object and the formal object precisely.
   190	  \item Freeze a source-faithful definition or state an adapter theorem
   191	  relating the existing definition to the source object.
   192	  \item Recheck the downstream theorem chain against that definition or adapter.
   193	  \item Re-formalize the affected subtree from the corrected interface, rather
   194	  than adding local hypotheses to each downstream theorem.
   195	  \item If a downstream proof cannot be completed, record the missing obligation
   196	  at the lowest point where the paper proof needs it.
   197	\end{enumerate}
   198	
   199	This is slower than editing a final theorem signature, but it prevents a local
   200	definition error from becoming a global theorem-statement error.
   201	
   202	\section{Allowed shapes}
   203	
   204	\begin{center}
   205	\begin{tabular}{p{0.24\linewidth}p{0.31\linewidth}p{0.32\linewidth}}
   206	\textbf{Shape} & \textbf{Allowed use} & \textbf{Forbidden use} \\
   207	\hline
   208	Paper-facing theorem & Matches the source statement up to faithful encoding &
   209	Carries non-paper bridge, residual, repair, input, obligation-structure, or
   210	proof-obligation hypotheses \\
   211	Source-shaped theorem with a tracked \verb|sorry| & Default repair when the
   212	source proof is blocked but the statement is known & Replaced by a strengthened
   213	theorem statement merely to keep the file compiling \\
   214	Conditional helper & Temporary quarantine for substantial proof content whose
   215	remaining named obligation has not yet been discharged & Introduced merely to
   216	avoid a \verb|sorry|, or linked as the source theorem or marked as
   217	proof-complete for that theorem \\
   218	Obligation discharger theorem & Constructs the obligation from paper hypotheses &
   219	Merely restates the obligation as an assumption \\
   220	Input bundle & Collects produced data for a local construction & Is assumed by a
   221	source theorem instead of being produced \\
   222	Obligation structure & Bundles constructed data and estimates & Hides unproved
   223	fields that are then assumed by a source theorem \\
   224	Paper-gap note & Documents a real mathematical or formal-statement divergence &
   225	Justifies silent statement drift without a repair plan
   226	\end{tabular}
   227	\end{center}
   228	
   229	\section{Protocol for a blocked proof}
   230	
   231	When a source-labelled proof is blocked, use the following order.
   232	
   233	\begin{enumerate}
   234	  \item Read the cited source statement and the proof passage in
   235	  \path{references/ldt-paper/}.
   236	  \item Write the paper theorem form, the current \Lean{} theorem form, and the
